figures.caption: Fig. 1 | Operando single-particle XRD for measuring reaction heterogeneity in thick electrode at high voltage. a, Cross-sectional SEM image of a slurry-processed NMC811 cathode with a total electrode thickness of ~125 um. b, A schematic of the operando single-particle XRD setup using high-flux synchrotron radiation. c, Voltage profile for the slurry-processed NMC811 cathode during charging to 4.70 V versus Li metal anode at C/10-rate (charge capacity ~250 mAh/g). d,e, Tracked c-lattice parameters from the (003) Bragg peak position (d) and (003) Bragg peak widths (e) for four representative particles, reflecting ASYNCHRONOUS phase transitions. [our note] d/e = the direct evidence that individual particles in a thick electrode sit at different states of charge -- justification for our STEP4 per-particle split.

Fig. 2 | Impact of reaction heterogeneity in slurry-processed thick electrode on optimizing active material ratio at high voltage. a, Angularly averaged diffraction patterns along the Debye-Scherrer ring under different charging voltage; x-axis is converted to c (A), 13-15. Arrows mark the pseudo-peak accompanying the (003) splitting (from 4.40 V). b, Voltage profiles of slurry-processed NMC811 thick electrodes with 93/95/97 wt% active material, 4.70-2.50 V vs Li at C/10 (x-axis = x in LixNi0.8Mn0.1Co0.1O2). Inset = the 4.6-4.7 V polarization/fluctuation of the 97 wt% electrode. [our note] this is the quantitative basis for the slurry wt% ceiling (~97 wt%): reversible capacity 220 -> 200 mAh/g from 93 -> 97 wt%.

Fig. 3 | Architecture design and modelling verification of dry-processed thick electrode for high-voltage stability. a, Schematic of the composite thick electrode (NMC, carbon fibres CF, PTFE). b,c, Initial and final state of the CGMD box. d, VGCF-PTFE radial distribution function g_ij + coordination number. e, Probability density of PTFE radius of gyration (RoG), initial vs final. f, Interchain distance between a VGCF pair vs simulation time. [our note] CRITICAL: panels b/c show that the CGMD box contains ONLY VGCF (grey rods) and PTFE (yellow beads) -- there is NO active material, no compaction, and no conductivity is computed. Digitized: RDF peak 8.7 -> 11.8 at r~60 nm (2nd shoulder ~11.5 at ~72 nm); coordination number at r=150 nm 11 -> 20; RoG peak 0.036@~60 nm -> 0.042@~46 nm; interfibre distance 361 -> 253 nm and STILL DECREASING at the end of the run (not converged). Stated protocol sums to 445 ns but the x-axis runs to ~660 ns (unreconciled).

Fig. 4 | Connectivity evaluation of the electronically conductive network for both dry- and slurry-processed thick electrodes with areal loading of ~30 mg/cm2. a,b, Segmented PFIB-SEM images of dry- (a) and slurry-processed (b) electrodes, NMC811 red, CBD dark blue, pores light blue. c,d, Connectivity maps of the CBD network (each colour = one isolated CBD aggregate), dry (c) and slurry (d). e,f, Simulated current density distribution at C/3 flowing top to bottom, dry (e) and slurry (f); colour bar log10(J [A/m2]) -10...+10. [our note] THE decisive figure. c/d give the headline 61.2 % (dry) vs 17.1 % (slurry) largest connected CBD cluster; e/f visualise that slurry forces current through the poorly conducting NMC (average particle current density 1.0e-2 vs 4.6e-5 A/m2, 217x). See card section 3-3: our re-analysis of the authors' Source Data gives 1.40x (not 3.58x) for the 3D per-slice statistics.

Fig. 5 | Electrochemical performances of dry-processed thick electrode demonstrating high-voltage stability and maximized active material content. a, Voltage profiles of dry-processed NMC811 thick electrodes (~30 mg/cm2) with 93/95/97 wt% active material, 4.70-2.50 V vs Li at C/10; inset shows the SMOOTH high-voltage region for 97 wt% (contrast Fig. 2b). b, 99 wt% electrode at C/10 and C/3. c, Cycling of the 99 wt% electrode at C/3 vs Li (4.3 V cutoff, liquefied gas electrolyte): 92 % over 200 cycles, average CE > 99.7 %. d, Literature summary (active material ratio vs reversible capacity, bubble size = mass loading bands L>50 / 50>L>30 / 30>L>20 / 20>L>10 / 10>L mg/cm2). [our note] d is a useful design-space map.

Fig. 6 | Comparison of electrochemical performance and post-mortem analysis of thick electrode applied in NMC811||graphite full cells highlighting the high-voltage stability of dry-processed electrodes. a, Cycling of full cells using 95 wt% NMC811 cathodes (~5 mAh/cm2) at C/3: slurry PC 4.70 V, dry PC 4.70 V, dry SC 4.70 V, dry SC 4.55 V (the 4.55 V case is a POUCH cell, the other three are coin cells). b,d, Aberration-corrected STEM-HAADF of NMC811 after 100 cycles, slurry (b) and dry (d). c,e, Spatially resolved O K-edge EELS from surface to bulk, slurry (c) and dry (e). f, ICP-MS of cycled graphite anodes. [our note] b/d give CEI > 5 nm (slurry, porous/discontinuous) vs ~2 nm (dry, compact). f digitized by us: Ni 0.89 vs 0.40, Mn 0.20 vs 0.043, Co 0.046 vs 0.016 ppm (slurry vs dry; total ~1.14 vs ~0.46 ppm, 2.5x) -- the paper states only 'substantially higher, primarily Ni'.

figures.label: S1
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 1. The powder X-ray diffraction pattern of as-received NMC811 and Rietveld refinement confirms phase purity and low cation disorder. Refinement was performed using a layered–type structure (space group R-3m). The background was modeled using a polynomial, and peak profiles were fitted with a pseudo-Voigt function to account for instrumental broadening. Scale factor, lattice parameters, zero shift, and peak shape parameters were refined sequentially, followed by refinement of atomic positions and site occupancies.

figures.label: S2
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 2. SEM images of as-received NMC811 powder at different magnifications. Low-magnification SEM image (left) showing uniform spherical secondary particles with diameters ranging from ~5-15 μm. High-magnification SEM image (right) reveals the polycrystalline nature of the secondary particles, consisting of densely packed primary crystallites with lateral dimensions of 100-500 nm.

figures.label: S3
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 3. SEM images of selected VGCF (A, C), highlighting its high-aspect-ratio morphology. SEM images of PTFE binder (B, D) at different magnifications, showing the initial particulate morphology prior to shear-induced fibrillation during dry processing.

figures.label: S4
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 4. XPS analysis of VGCF before and after dry mixing with PTFE under shearing stress. Solid lines overlaid on the experimental data represent fitted component peaks obtained using CasaXPS software. Peak fitting was performed after Shirley background subtraction using mixed Gaussian–Lorentzian line shapes, with full width at half maximum and peak positions constrained consistently across samples to enable quantitative comparison of surface chemical states. The shift in the O 1s peak from 533 eV to 531 eV after dry mixing with PTFE under shearing stress, while the C 1s peak remains unchanged—indicating a transformation in surface oxygen species. This shift suggests two possibilities: 1) structural transformation of oxygen species, such as C-O to C=O, leading to lower binding energy; or 2) partial charge transfer from the binder to oxygen. figures.label: S5
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 5. XPS O 1s spectra deconvolution of VGCF before and after dry mixing with PTFE under shearing stress. Solid lines overlaid on the experimental data represent fitted component peaks obtained using CasaXPS software. Peak fitting was performed after Shirley background subtraction using mixed Gaussian–Lorentzian line shapes. The deconvoluted O 1s spectrum was resolved into different components corresponding to oxygen species in different chemical environments. The percentage values indicate the relative area fractions of each component. Peak positions and full width at half maximum were constrained consistently across samples to enable quantitative comparison of surface chemical states.

figures.label: S6
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 6. Schematic illustration of the proposed interfacial interaction mechanism between VGCF and PTFE. Before shear mixing (A), surface oxygen functional groups on VGCF are predominantly in the enol form (C-OH). After shear mixing with PTFE (B), these groups undergo an enol-to-keto transition to form C=O species, promoting chemical coupling between VGCF and the fibrillated PTFE binder.

figures.label: S7
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 7. Raman analysis of VGCF before and after dry mixing with PTFE under shearing stress. The spectra in (B) are a magnified view of the 2D′ region in (A), emphasizing changes in the 2D′ features associated with surface chemical transformation induced by shear mixing.

figures.label: S8
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 8. SEM images of VGCF and PTFE binder after shear mixing in the dry- processed electrode at different magnifications. Images in the left panel (A, C) were acquired with the T2 detector, whereas those in the right panel (B, D) were obtained with the T3 detector for the same areas of interest.

figures.label: S9
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 9. Relative CBD distribution along the thickness direction as a function of distance from the current collector for dry-processed (left) and slurry-processed (right) thick electrodes. Errors represent one standard deviation calculated from spatially resolved CBD area fractions measured across multiple PFIB-SEM cross-sectional slices at each distance from the current collector.

figures.label: S10
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 10. The reconstructed CBD network for both slurry-processed (left) and dry- processed (right) thick electrode through 3D PFIB tomography. Different colors represent distinct, mutually disconnected CBD sub-networks, where all voxels sharing the same color belong to a single continuous conductive cluster.

figures.label: S11
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 11. The distribution of the normalized largest percolating CBD network fraction across all reconstructed PFIB-SEM slices for slurry- and dry-processed electrodes. Mean value is defined as arithmetic average of the normalized largest CBD network fraction across slices; higher mean value indicates stronger dominance of a connected CBD network within slices. Median value is defined as 50th percentile (middle value). Min value is defined as minimum observed value across slices; weakest in-plane connectivity slice in the dataset. Max value is defined as maximum observed value across slices; strongest in-plane connectivity slice in the dataset. [our note] VIOLIN plot; the numeric values are NOT printed. Its Source Data (MOESM5, sheet Distribution_Data) gives Slurry n=135 mean 0.3836 sd(pop) 0.1383 [0.1633, 0.7796] and Dry n=121 mean 0.5359 sd(pop) 0.0985 [0.2683, 0.9382] -> mean ratio 1.397. Note the SLURRY violin is visibly BIMODAL (~30 % and ~50 % lobes) while the dry one is unimodal -- which is why a single 2D cross-section can land anywhere and why the 2D headline (17.1 vs 61.2 %) exaggerates the 3D contrast.

figures.label: S12
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 12. Relative pores distribution along the thickness direction as a function of distance from the current collector for dry-processed (left) and slurry-processed (right) thick electrodes. Errors represent one standard deviation calculated from spatially resolved pores area fractions measured across multiple PFIB-SEM cross-sectional slices at each distance from the current collector.

figures.label: S13
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 13. Relative effective diffusivity of Li+ as a function of tortuosity factor for slurry-processed and dry-processed thick electrodes. The effective diffusivity was calculated by combining the measured porosity and tortuosity obtained from segmented PFIB-SEM reconstructions, assuming identical intrinsic electrolyte diffusivity in both electrodes. The dry- processed electrode exhibits a higher effective Li⁺ diffusivity, reflecting reduced tortuosity and more efficient ionic transport pathways through the electrolyte phase. [our note] the tortuosity convention lives here: only D_eff ~ eps/tau^2 reproduces the paper's stated '~33 %' from tau 2.87 -> 2.49 (+32.9 %); the TauFactor convention D_eff = eps*D/tau gives +15.3 %.

figures.label: S14
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 14. LSV measurements of the dry-processed and slurry-processed carbon and binder composite until 4.8 V versus Li metal anode. Note the 3.9 V oxidation peak for slurry- processed sample is attributed to early-onset Al current collector corrosion and electrolyte reactions. As reported,16 Al foils in LiPF6–carbonate electrolytes begin to undergo pitting corrosion just above ~3.8–4.0 V. In our slurry-cast PTFE/PVDF control sample (which contains no active material), the film is relatively sparse — increasing the likelihood of local pinholes that expose bare Al directly to electrolyte, thereby triggering this Al–electrolyte reaction around 3.9 V. [our note] the authors themselves attribute the slurry 3.9 V oxidation peak to Al current-collector pitting, not to the binder -- so the LSV contrast is partly confounded.

figures.label: S17
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 17. Angularly averaged operando single-particle X-ray diffraction patterns along the Debye−Scherrer ring under different charging voltage for the dry-processed NMC811 cathode. Measurements were performed in a cell using a Li metal as counter electrode with the cathode charged to 4.7 V at a C/10-rate.

figures.label: S18
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 18. Nyquist fitting plots of half-cells cycled with a charging cutoff voltage of 4.7 V for dry-processed (A) and slurry-processed (B) NMC811 thick electrodes. Solid lines overlaid on the experimental data represent fitted curves based on an equivalent circuit model as shown in each plot. Fitting was performed over the full frequency range using ZView, with all parameters allowed to vary within physically reasonable bounds.

figures.label: S19
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 19. Optical images demonstrating scalable fabrication and mechanical robustness of the dry-processed electrode with 99 wt% active material content. The left panel (A) shows a free-standing electrode film with an area of approximately 25 cm2, highlighting uniform thickness. The right panel (B) shows the free-standing film under bending, confirming excellent flexibility and the absence of visible cracking, indicative of sufficient mechanical cohesion for roll-to-roll manufacturing and practical cell assembly.

figures.label: S20
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 20. Representative stress-strain curves of dry-processed thick electrodes with various active material content. Despite increasing the active material fraction from 93 wt% to 99 wt%, the electrodes retain comparable tensile strength, indicating preserved mechanical integrity and sufficient cohesion for handling and cell assembly even at ultra-high active material ratios.

figures.label: S21
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 21. Rate performance of the dry-processed thick electrode with 99 wt% active material content evaluated at various current densities. Cells were assembled using lithium metal as the counter electrode with a cathode areal loading of approximately 30 mg/cm2. Galvanostatic charge–discharge tests were conducted at progressively increasing current densities, as indicated in the plot, within a voltage up to 4.7 V.

figures.label: S22
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 22. Segmented PFIB-SEM images and contact area analysis of dry-processed electrodes, with the NMC811 in red, the CBD in dark blue, and the pores in light blue. The contact fraction was extracted from segmented PFIB-SEM cross-sectional images by identifying pixels at direct NMC–CBD interfaces and normalizing by the total NMC surface area.

figures.label: S23
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 23. The voltage profile of the dry-processed NMC811 cathode with 99.5 wt% active material charged to 4.7 V versus Li metal anode at C/10-rate.

figures.label: S24
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 24. Comparison of Coulombic efficiency of thick electrode (areal loading of ~5 mAh/cm2) applied in NMC811||graphite full cells cycled at C/3-rate.

figures.label: S25
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 25. Cycling performance of NMC811||graphite full cells using 95 wt% dry- processed cathodes at C/3-rate and 50 ℃ with a charging cutoff voltage of 4.7 V.

figures.label: S26
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 26. SEM images of as-received single-crystal NMC811 particles at different magnifications. The low-magnification image (A) shows well-defined, faceted particles with uniform morphology and narrow size distribution. The higher-magnification image (B) highlights the absence of secondary particles, distinguishing from conventional polycrystalline samples.

figures.label: S27
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 27. Voltage profiles of the dry-processed thick electrode (~30 mg/cm2) evaluated at various cutoff voltages with Li metal anode. Cells were cycled at a C/10-rate. The profiles illustrate the systematic increase in delivered capacity and discharge energy density with increasing cutoff voltage, providing the basis for assessing the trade-off between energy density and long-term cycling stability.

figures.label: S28
figures.caption: Supplementary Fig. 28. SEM images of pristine (A) and cycled graphite anode (B). EDX quantification of the regions marked in the SEM images of the pristine and cycled graphite electrodes. The pristine electrode displays only C (99.9 at%) and trace O (0.1 at%) signals consistent with native surface oxidation. After long-term cycling in the FEC-based electrolyte, the graphite surface exhibits clear F (17.9 at%) and P (1.0 at%) signatures originating from electrolyte and salt decomposition, confirming the formation of a fluorine- and phosphorus-containing solid electrolyte interphase. Note the reported atomic percentage value reflects the average across all measured spots.
